paper.title: Hardness of Online Sleeping Combinatorial Optimization Problems

settings.name_in_paper: Online sleeping combinatorial optimization (per-action regret) (lower bound)
unmapped: Sleeping elements S_t are revealed at the start of each round; awake actions are those avoiding S_t
Per-action regret: regret against action V summed only over rounds in which V is awake
Losses and availabilities drawn jointly i.i.d. from a fixed unknown distribution (SLA); hardness also holds for worst-case adversary
Computational (not information-theoretic) lower bound: applies to polynomial-time learners under hardness of PAC learning DNF
settings.definition_quote: In this setting, at the start of each round $t$, the adversary selects a set of \emph{sleeping elements} $S_t \subseteq U$ and reveals it to the learner. Define $\A_t = \{V \in \D ~|~ V \cap S_t = \emptyset\}$, the set of \emph{awake actions} at round $t$ ... Per-action regret with respect to $V \in \D$ is defined as: \Regret_T(V) := \sum_{t:\, V \in \A_t} \ell_t(V_t) - \ell_t(V).

symbols.poly_d: an arbitrary polynomially bounded function of d

conditions: algorithm runs in time poly(T, d)
conditional on PAC learning DNF expressions being computationally hard (reduction via online agnostic learning of disjunctions)
problem admits a hard instance (heaviness and richness properties) for every n, with 3n+2 <= d <= poly(n)

source.label: thm:main
source.quote: Consider an online sleeping combinatorial optimization problem such that for any positive integer $n$, there is a hard instance with parameter $n$ of the problem. Suppose there is an algorithm $\algosco$ that for any instance of the problem with ground set $U$ of size $d$, runs in time $\poly(T, d)$ and has regret bounded by $\poly(d) \cdot T^{1-\delta}$ for some $\delta \in (0, 1)$. Then, there exists an algorithm $\algdisj$ for online agnostic learning of disjunctions over $n$ variables with running time $\poly(T,n)$ and regret $\poly(n) \cdot T^{1-\delta}$.

results.notes: This is a reduction or hardness statement, not an explicit regret bound. Figure 1 summarises it as a computational lower bound Omega(poly(d) T^{1-delta}) under the SLA assumption: no efficient algorithm achieves no per-action regret unless DNF is efficiently PAC learnable. Section 5 applies it to the sleeping versions of Online Shortest Path (Sabotaged Shortest Path), Minimum Spanning Tree, k-Subsets, k-Truncated Permutations, Bipartite Matching and Minimum Cut. The paper remarks that it extends to ranking and policy regret. The quantity is set to 'other' because the guarantee does not fit any standard type.
